# Engine shakes, from bad oil change

The symptoms you are describingâexcessive idle shake and a history of an unsecured dipstickâare classic indicators that lubricant has migrated into areas where it doesn't belong. When a dipstick is not fastened properly, or if the filler cap seal was compromised during service, gravity does the rest. Oil flows from the reservoir down through the crankcase ventilation system or directly over component surfaces until it reaches the lowest points in the engine bay. In your case, that bottom line includes the spark plug wells and the plugs themselves.

The immediate concern regarding engine damage is understandable, but the physics of the situation suggests a specific failure mode rather than catastrophic internal destruction. You noted there is no knock and the car runs, which eliminates major bearing failures or piston slap. However, the presence of oil on the bottom of the spark plugs, specifically where they screw in, changes the combustion dynamics significantly.

Spark plugs function by creating a high-voltage arc across an air-fuel mixture inside the cylinder. For this to happen efficiently, the insulator tip and the electrode must remain dry. When oil coats the threads or the underside of the plug, it creates a conductive path that can short out the ignition coil. In modern vehicles with direct ignition coils mounted over the plugs (coil-on-plug), this is particularly risky. If the oil bridges the gap between the high-voltage terminal and the engine block, you will see misfires. The engine control unit (ECU) detects these misfires as a lack of cylinder contribution, which manifests physically as the shaking you feel at idle.

The question of whether the plugs are flooded requires a distinction between liquid fuel and liquid oil. "Flooded" usually refers to an excess of gasoline in the cylinder, preventing ignition. In your scenario, you likely have a wet plug condition caused by oil ingress. Even if you clean the exterior of the engine bay and the spark plug wells, removing all oil residues is difficult once they have seeped into the insulator pores or coated the threads. Cleaning with standard solvents might remove surface oil, but it does not restore the electrical insulation properties lost to contamination.

Given that you cleaned everything to the best of your ability, the logical next step involves replacing the affected spark plugs. This is not just a precaution; it is a necessary repair to restore proper combustion efficiency. When installing new plugs, ensure the threads are clean and free of any oily residue before threading them into the cylinder head. Using anti-seize compound on the threads can help prevent galling during installation, but avoid applying it to the insulator tip or electrodes, as this can affect the gap and voltage requirements.

Regarding the source of the leak, an unfastened dipstick is a procedural error that needs correction. Before replacing parts, verify that the oil filler cap and the dipstick tube seal are intact. If the dipstick was simply loose and not damaged, tightening it should stop future leaks. However, if you observed oil spewing, there may have been significant pressure buildup or a cracked O-ring on the crankcase breather system (PCV valve). Inspect the PCV valve; if it is clogged or sticking, it can create excessive crankcase pressure, forcing oil past seals and gaskets indiscriminately.

There is no evidence from your description to suggest the engine block itself is damaged internally. The shake is almost certainly a combustion efficiency issue resulting from wet plugs causing misfires. Replacing the plugs and ensuring the ventilation system is clear should resolve the vibration. If the shaking persists after replacement, scan the vehicle for trouble codes. Look specifically for P0300 (random/multiple cylinder misfire) or cylinder-specific codes like P0301-P0304. These codes will confirm whether the ECU has already logged the performance loss caused by the oil contamination.

If you are maintaining a fleet of vehicles or managing a workshop, this incident highlights the importance of torque specifications and seal verification during routine maintenance. A simple oversight on a dipstick can lead to complex diagnostic paths involving spark plug replacement and potential coil pack damage. Always inspect the crankcase venting system after any oil service to ensure no leaks are introduced or exacerbated by the procedure.
